Uber faces investor questions on autonomous vehicles ahead of earnings Proactive uses images sourced from Shutterstock

Uber Technologies Inc (NYSE:UBER, XETRA:UT8) heads into its third-quarter results with investor attention focused on its autonomous vehicle supply pipeline, which Bank of America sees as the biggest factor shaping sentiment towards the ride-hailing company.

The broker expects Uber's gross bookings to reach $59.8 billion and adjusted earnings before interest, tax, depreciation and amortisation (EBITDA) to total $2.94 billion, broadly in line with Wall Street forecasts of $2.93 billion in EBITDA.

The gross bookings estimate represents 21% year-on-year growth on a constant-currency basis, a one-percentage-point slowdown from the second quarter, BofA said.

The bank expects fourth-quarter gross bookings guidance of $62.75 billion to $64.75 billion, with adjusted earnings per share of $0.96 to $1, ranges that bracket consensus estimates of $64.3 billion and $0.98 respectively.

Share buybacks and cost-saving measures, including job cuts, could support earnings, although higher petrol prices could increase driver costs and put pressure on margins.

BofA expects adjusted earnings per share to grow 27% in 2027 and maintained its $101 price target, based on 23 times forecast 2027 earnings.

The broker said Uber's valuation looked attractive at about 10 times analysts' 2027 EBITDA and price-to-free-cash-flow estimates, leaving room for its valuation multiple to expand if progress on autonomous vehicles improves investor confidence.

Competition from autonomous-driving services, including reported expansion plans by Waymo and Tesla's Cybercab programme, has weighed on the shares, making updates on US vehicle supply and partnerships a central focus of the results call.

BofA said an update on Uber's autonomous-vehicle supply pipeline, potentially including progress linked to Nvidia, could help sentiment, while risks include higher investment spending, elevated petrol prices, disruption from protests in Europe and potential market-share losses to Lyft.

title: Wall Street’s Borrowing Binge Is Slowing, and BofA Says That Can Signal a Top
detail:
Wall Street’s Borrowing Binge Is Slowing, and BofA Says That Can Signal a Top
Omor Ibne Ehsan

BAC
SPY
HOOD

Quick Read

BofA's Paul Ciana warns margin debt growth falling from 54% to 31% mirrors slowdowns that preceded the 2000, 2007, and 2021 market peaks.

The largest triple-leveraged semiconductor ETF drew $9 billion in two weeks, a record, while retail traders now account for 61% of options volume on one major platform.

HOOD is down 35% over the past year while SPY is up 13% year to date with less exposure to retail borrowing.

Just released. Our analysts combed the entire stock market and named the ten best stocks to buy right now, and Bank of America didn't make the cut. Enter your email to see the names that beat BAC. The report is free. Enter your email and see if any of your stocks made the cut.

At the end of September, Americans who borrow against their stocks owed their brokers about $1.48 trillion, close to a record. That debt has held up, but its growth has slowed sharply.

Lightspring / Shutterstock.com

In a note dated October 23, 2026, Bank of America (NYSE:BAC) technical strategist Paul Ciana said year-over-year margin debt growth fell to 31.4% in September, down from 53.7% in May. He said that when growth cools off after an extreme run, the slowdown has lined up with past market peaks and can signal a top. He framed the slowdown as a warning sign of elevated risk.

Both the broad market and the retail broker rose after the warning. SPDR S&P 500 ETF Trust (NYSEARCA:SPY) rose 0.57% to 769.66 on October 27. Robinhood Markets (NASDAQ:HOOD) gained 1.85% to $94.56 on the same day it reported a record margin book that is growing much more slowly.

Why BofA Pays Attention to Slowing Growth

BofA ranked May's growth rate fourth-highest since 1998. The only higher levels came in 2000, 2007 and 2021, and a stock decline followed each one.

The total itself is still rising. September balances rose 1.80% from August and sit 1.47% below June's high. The growth rate, however, has fallen.

The pace matters more than the total because each new dollar of margin debt is new buying power. When that new borrowing slows, the market loses a source of demand. If prices then fall, margin calls (demands from brokers for more cash or collateral) push borrowers to sell into the decline. Riding a late-cycle rally is fine as long as the exit is planned, which is the whole subject of our free bubble survivor's handbook.

Ciana raised this risk before. On June 29, with growth near 54%, he wrote that "U.S. equities could face a corrective phase in the third quarter." He also pointed to an opposing pattern: "Typically, risk assets such as the S&P 500 rebound after midterms unless more severe downside risks materialize."

Leverage Is Moving Into Funds and Options

Over one month, the ten largest leveraged equity ETFs took in $12 billion of new money while their market value fell $20 billion. The largest triple-leveraged semiconductor fund drew $9 billion in two weeks, the biggest two-week inflow in its history.

These funds borrow internally to deliver two or three times an index's daily return, so investors get leverage without a margin loan showing up in brokerage data. Options work the same way, because a small premium controls a large position. Retail traders recently made up 61% of options volume on one large market maker's platform.

Robinhood's Margin Growth Has Slowed Sharply

Robinhood's margin book hit a record $22.1 billion in the third quarter. Year-over-year growth slowed to 59% from 127% in the second quarter, and the book stands only 2.3% above its June level.

Revenue rose 12% to $1.42 billion. Diluted EPS fell 16% to $0.51, and net interest revenue fell 9% to $415 million.

The Fed announces its rate decision on October 28, with the upper bound of its target range at 4.00%. A rate cut reduces the margin borrowers pay, and it also cuts Robinhood's interest income. Management estimates that each quarter-point move changes revenue by about 1.5%.

HOOD Earnings Explorer — 24/7 Wall St.
What Robinhood's Slowing Margin Book Means for HOOD Stock
HOOD Price Target — 24/7 Wall St.

We believe the stock has more downside risk. The stock trades between a 52-week low of $63.52 and a high of $150.47, and it is down 35.17% over the past year.

That decline shows some slowing, but the price still shows a margin book that stops growing while rates fall. Trading volumes early in the fourth quarter were already about 5% lighter than in the third quarter.

SPY has held up better. It is up 12.87% year to date, and it tracks the broad market that Ciana said typically rebounds after midterms, with less exposure to retail borrowing.

Two data points would show whether this view is wrong. If FINRA's October margin data moves above June's high, or if Robinhood's fourth-quarter margin book rises clearly above $22.1 billion, the borrowing cycle is still running.

In ETFs, tech funds saw the largest inflows. The bank also highlighted a shift in factor flows.

title: BAC's NII Growth Accelerates in 2026: Is the Stock Worth Buying Now?
detail:
BAC's NII Growth Accelerates in 2026: Is the Stock Worth Buying Now?
Nikita Kataruka
Wed, October 28, 2026 at 10:26 AM EDT 8 min read
BAC
JPM
C
Explore stocks on Coinbase
Trading disclosure

Bank of America BAC has sustained robust net interest income (NII) growth so far this year, driven by healthy loan and deposit expansion, fixed-rate asset repricing and higher contributions from Global Markets activities. The banking giant's improving NII trajectory underscores its balance-sheet strength and ability to navigate a shifting rate environment.

After rising 7.1% year over year to $15.75 billion in the first quarter, BAC's NII increased 9% to $16 billion in the second quarter. The momentum extended into the third quarter, with NII advancing 8% to a record $16.45 billion. The net interest yield expanded 15 basis points year over year to 2.16% in the third quarter, while ending loans and leases grew 7% to $1.25 trillion, reinforcing the bank's interest-earning capacity.

Looking ahead, BAC remains optimistic about sustaining the NII momentum, with management projecting NII growth of 8% in 2026 and at least 8% in 2027. Continued balance-sheet expansion and favorable fixed-rate asset repricing are expected to underpin this growth, providing a tailwind to profitability despite interest-rate uncertainties.

With NII momentum strengthening and a favorable growth outlook, does BAC present a compelling investment opportunity at the current levels? While improving interest income strengthens the investment case, an assessment of the bank's other fundamental strengths, potential headwinds and valuation is essential before making any investment decision.

BAC's Other Key Positives to Note:

Accelerating Digital & AI-Led Transformation: Bank of America continues to invest in digital banking, artificial intelligence (AI), payments infrastructure and branch expansion to strengthen customer engagement and operating efficiency. The bank plans to open at least 20 additional financial centers by year-end, following 14 openings in the third quarter.

The growing adoption of its AI-powered virtual assistant Erica and Zelle, alongside generative AI integration, is expected to enhance productivity and lower servicing costs. Meanwhile, investments in Swift and CashPro are strengthening its global payments capabilities, while the proposed Jio Credit investment offers exposure to India's expanding digital lending market.

Management expects benefits from its AI initiatives to rise from $250-$300 million in 2026 to $700 million in 2027. These investments should drive efficiency gains, diversify revenue opportunities and support long-term earnings growth.

Industry-Leading Deposit Franchise: Bank of America continues to benefit from its extensive, low-cost deposit franchise, providing a competitive advantage and a stable funding base. As of Sept. 30, 2026, loans and leases grew 7% year over year to $1.25 trillion, while deposits rose 1.8% to $2.04 trillion. Non-interest-bearing deposits contributed more than 75% to third-quarter deposit growth, with the average deposit rate remaining low at 1.49%.

BAC's diversified deposit base and favorable loan-to-deposit ratio provide flexibility to fund lending growth while limiting reliance on costly wholesale funding. These strengths, coupled with disciplined deposit pricing, should support NII growth, margins and profitability.

Robust Investment Banking (IB) Franchise: Bank of America's IB franchise continues to benefit from improving capital markets activity and a healthy deal pipeline. Following declines of 45.7% in 2022 and 2.4% in 2023, IB fees rebounded and grew 31.4% in 2024 and another 8.4% in 2025. The recovery continued in the first nine months of 2026, with IB fees rising 14.6% year over year.

While the company's third-quarter 2026 IB fees (excluding self-led deals) declined 11% year over year (reflecting softer advisory and debt underwriting activity), management remains optimistic about its robust deal pipeline. It continues to invest in bankers, technology and AI capabilities to strengthen execution and client engagement.

Looking ahead, a potential recovery in mergers and acquisitions (M&A), improving corporate confidence and stronger capital-raising activity should support fee income growth and earnings diversification, although elevated interest rates and geopolitical uncertainties remain near-term headwinds.

Robust Capital Returns Strategy: Bank of America continues to demonstrate its commitment to enhancing shareholder returns through consistent dividend growth and share repurchases. Following its successful performance in the 2026 Federal Reserve stress test, the bank increased its quarterly dividend 14.3% to 32 cents per share, marking its sixth consecutive annual dividend hike.

The company maintains an active capital return program, distributing $8.3 billion to shareholders in the third quarter of 2026, including $6 billion through share repurchases and $2.2 billion in common stock dividends.

Its common equity tier 1 (CET1) ratio stood at 10.9% as of Sept. 30, 2026, remaining above regulatory requirements. Supported by strong capital ratios, resilient earnings and excess capital generation, Bank of America remains well-positioned to sustain attractive shareholder distributions while supporting business growth.

Trading disclosure

Citigroup Inc. C continues to demonstrate meaningful improvement in profitability, supported by robust revenue growth, operating efficiency gains and disciplined execution of its transformation initiatives. In the first nine months of 2026, return on tangible common equity (RoTCE) improved 400 basis points (bps) year over year to 12.6%, underscoring the company's strengthening earnings-generating capabilities and progress toward achieving sustainable returns.

The profitability improvement was driven by broad-based growth across Citigroup's core businesses. Meanwhile, operating expenses increased a modest 3% to $42.48 billion, significantly below the pace of revenue growth. Consequently, the efficiency ratio improved to 58% from 63.2% in the year-ago period, highlighting positive operating leverage and improving cost efficiency.

Looking ahead, Citigroup's diversified revenue streams, ongoing business simplification and disciplined capital allocation are expected to support profitability. Management anticipates 2026 RoTCE above 11%, while targeting 11-13% for 2027-2028. Continued expansion in fee-generating businesses, improving operating leverage and shareholder-friendly capital distributions could further strengthen its earnings outlook. However, elevated credit costs, transformation-related expenses and macroeconomic uncertainty remain the key challenges.

Against this backdrop, should investors continue holding on to the C stock to capitalize on its improving fundamentals? Let us delve deeper to answer this.

Citigroup's Performance Catalysts

Strategic Streamlining Efforts: Citigroup has moved closer to completing its multi-year exit from non-core international consumer banking. The sale of the Polish consumer business in June 2026 marked the final international consumer divestiture apart from remaining wind-downs of Banamex. The company also sold an additional 22.6% stake in Banamex in the second quarter after selling 25% in late 2025. The remaining Banamex deconsolidation and IPO are planned for early 2027, with management expecting the transaction to free up $5 billion in capital.

These transactions follow the completed Russia exit and divestitures of consumer franchises across Asia and EMEA. The simpler structure reduces operational complexity, releases capital and allows management to direct resources toward Services, Markets, Banking, Wealth and U.S. Consumer Cards. During the second-quarter earnings call, management highlighted continued investment in U.S. Consumer Cards, including product development, partnerships and customer acquisition.

However, the estimate reductions do not change the firm's positive view on off-price retail stocks, which are expected to outperform as inflation constrains consumer purchasing power.

2. Ross Stores (ROST) - The retailer saw its fiscal 2027 estimates cut by 3% to account for higher freight expenses. Bank of America maintained its Buy rating on the stock, viewing the company as well-positioned to benefit from value-seeking consumer behavior in an inflationary environment.

3. TJX Companies (TJX) - Analysts reduced fiscal 2027 estimates for the off-price retailer by 3% due to anticipated margin pressure from elevated shipping costs. The firm reiterated its Buy rating intact, citing the company's ability to capitalize on trade-down trends as consumers face higher prices for necessities and persistently elevated fuel prices.

Bank of America now models a 15% increase in domestic freight and an 80% increase in ocean freight. The bank notes this environment remains more benign than 2022, when higher rates pressured margins by 200-300 basis points.

The analysts expect off-price retailers to continue outperforming as higher prices for necessities leave consumers with less to spend on discretionary goods, reinforcing value-seeking behavior that benefits the sector.
